subtopic: REPORT AS TO TRANSFER TO THE UNITED STATES OF BRITISH ORDER FOR A MILLION CASES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Compton (Mr. Blanchette) yesterday asked a question with regard to the report that there had been transferred to the United States an order for a million cases of condensed milk. I wish to answer as follows:
The dairy products board has no information of the transfer referred to. The ministry of food inquired about the purchases of a million cases of unsweetened condensed milk from Canada during the present fiscal year. However, they have stated that under no condition was there to be any large increase in unsweetened condensed milk sales to them if it would affect our available cheese supplies. Indications are that Canada will be in a position to supply approximately the same amount of unsweetened condensed milk to the ministry of food as was supplied last year and still take care of domestic and other export requirements. In 1940 the ministry of food purchased approximately 1,500,000 cases of such milk in the United States in addition to supplies from Canada and there is every reason to believe that the same will be done again this year.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
I suggest to the minister that subsection 2 is altogether too wide and that all but the first clause should be dropped. This section reads:
(1)	Every game officer shall, before entering upon the duties of his office, take and subscribe an oath . . .
(2)	Every game officer shall for all the purposes of this act have anywhere in Canada all the powers of a peace officer or a police constable . . .
I have not the slightest objection to that; I think it is quite proper. But then you go on and clothe these game officers with all the power and authority of a justice of the peace anywhere in Canada. This is what will happen. A game officer comes across an alleged

violation of this statute. He lays the charge, tries the culprit and collects the fine right on the spot. If hon. gentlemen have ever been caught in a violation of a traffic law in certain portions of the north American continent-

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: Speak for yourself.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
As a
matter of fact it did not happen to me, but it did happen to a friend of mine. I was not guilty this time, though I suppose I have transgressed the traffic laws on many occasions. A traffic officer stops a man for a violation of a traffic law and tells him that if he will give him $10 or $25, whatever it may be, it will be all right; apparently in some jurisdictions he has authority to do that. If a man is in a desperate hurry very often he will fall for that sort of thing and pay the ten dollars rather than stay over for a day and go to the police court, even though he may think he has a fair defence.
I do object to the principle underlying this section, that an officer charged with the enforcement of the law should be judge and jury and impose the penalty. It is bad principle and a very dangerous one, and I object to it. I shall not elaborate the reasons which underlie that statement, but I do appeal to the minister not to put through this provision. Let the ordinary operation of the law apply. We have plenty of laws to cover this sort of thing. Do not let the traffic officer or the game officer, as the case may be, act as judge on the facts and have complete jurisdiction to impose the penalty, so that perhaps an innocent person may suffer. The whole principle is wrong. I am not suggesting that the game officer may pocket the fees; that, of course would depend on the individual, though I have often wondered in the case of traffic violations whether moneys paid to these officers found their way into the public treasury.
This is an exceedingly bad principle; I do not think I ever saw it before in a federal statute. We have plenty of machinery for adjudicating upon these offences. Let them go through the ordinary process of law; let them be heard by a magistrate or a judicial officer who is not himself promoting the charge.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION

Has the dominion power to
confer this right on officers?

The hon. member raises a question of much greater academic importance, but I am trying to treat this matter realistically and press it home on a point which I am sure will appeal

to the minister as a layman. I have never looked into the question whether or not the dominion has power to appoint justices of the peace. In rare cases we do appoint king's counsel, but ordinarily the appointment of justices of the peace is done by the provinces. I think the dominion has authority to make these men peace officers, or rather to give them all the powers of peace officers, making them analogous to peace officers appointed by a province. But to say that this same man shall be the judge, when he is promoting the charge, is contrary to our sense of British justice. It is wrong. I hope the minister will reconsider this provision in the light of what I have said.

I too raised the point which has been raised by the leader of the opposition because to me, a layman, it appeared an unusual procedure. The purpose of including this power, one which is somewhat out of the ordinary, is to meet conditions which may arise in the more remote parts of the country.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: That is just a matter of expediency.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: Permit me to give an illustration. There may be a violation of the law in a remote part of northern Saskatchewan or Alberta. Any officer of the province, whether he be a mounted police officer or a game officer, is authorized under the measure, as I read it, to act as a magistrate in hearing a case which comes before him. In his capacity as law enforcement officer I believe it would not be possible for him to bring a case before himself as justice of the peace. In other words as justice of the peace he could not take evidence from himself in his capacity as law enforcement officer. But if there were two police officers in the circumstances I have mentioned, one could act as law enforcement officer and the other as justice of the peace.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: From the point of view of justice I do not think that has improved the situation very much.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: That is just the point: it will be put into effect in more thickly populated communities. I would say in the neighbouring country that is done every day, somewhere, in connection with breaches of traffic laws. That is an analogous position. I realize that there is some force in the minister's argument in respect of breaches of the law in more remote parts of the country. It is more difficult to have the machinery of the law operative in those parts. Per contra, however, it is much more difficult for an accused to defend himself under those circumstances. He would not have the benefit of the advice, to which he would be entitled, of any member of my profession. An innocent man could be at the mercy of an over-zealous or too officious law officer. It is of the protection and liberty of the subject, and his pocketbook, that I am thinking. There is a principle at stake, and the exceptional case to which the minister has referred should not be taken as governing the general rule.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION

I can recall an attempt of a somewhat similar nature when I sat in opposition, and I recall, too, that I condemned it at that time. For any police officer to be permitted to act also as judge and jury of an accused man is certainly a principle this house should not establish.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION

position as to the proposal embodied in this provision; it is indefensible, and with that statement I shall be content. I appeal to the minister's sense of justice. His desire to do the expedient thing should not overcome his sense of what is just and proper.

I have a right to take your plea of guilty, and I think it would be wise for you to plead guilty". In that way he could persuade the accused to plead guilty. Then he could fine him or impose a penalty. In such a case he would be acting as investigator, accuser, and judge, in his latter capacity imposing a penalty. It would be a terrible state of affairs.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: I can well understand the desire of the minister to clothe officers with extraordinary powers in isolated districts, but the power given a game warden under section 5, subsection 2, should be read in the light of sections 7, 8 and 9. In section 7 the game officer is given power to bring any person who has contravened the act before a justice of the peace. By section 8 we give any justice of the peace power to issue a search warrant, under the authority of which a game officer may enter a home or building at any hour of the day or night. By section 9 we give a justice of the peace power to issue a summons. Looking at it purely from the layman's point of view it seems to me that one game officer could clothe the other with authority to carry on a most extraordinary procedure. One game officer could issue a search warrant to another to search a home.

About three years ago-I believe, at the session of 1938- a bill was introduced and passed by the house controlling the export or the movement of furs from the northwest territories to Alberta and Saskatchewan. As I recall, the precise power was given there which is conveyed here, because of the possibility of pelts being transferred illegally from one province to another. A trapper came to Alberta with over 300 beaver skins which he had taken illegally in British Columbia. Having so

large a number of skins, he could hire an aeroplane and come with his freight of pelts to the airport near Edmonton. Under such circumstances, if a police officer at that point has reason to suspect that the pelts have been taken illegally, he can seize them immediately and hold them until the matter is settled by due process of law before a magistrate. If he has not the power to do that; if he has to go somewhere to get a search warrant before he can appropriate the skins, they may be half way to Calgary by the time he gets the search warrant, and thus the law is evaded.

Apparently this section has been drafted with a good deal of care. It reads:
(1) Any justice of the peace who is satisfied upon oath that there is reasonable ground for believing that there is in any store, shop, warehouse, outhouse, dwelling house, garden, yard, vessel, railway, vehicle, aircraft or other place game kept or concealed contrary to the provisions of this act may issue a warrant under his hand authorizing some constable or other person named therein to search such place by day or night for such game and to seize and bring it before the justice-
In circumstances such as the minister has suggested-in remote parts of the country a justice of the peace is not apt to be a highly trained man-I have often been bothered about the jurisdiction to issue a search warrant. I have heard of a justice of the peace issuing a search warrant on a mere verbal statement under oath. My own view is that the proper practice is that the statement shall be not only under oath but in writing, so that the writing may be available, in case of conviction, for review under writ of certiorari. Would the minister care to put the words "in writing"-in the section, to
indicate clearly the form in which the deposition must be made? That is what the trained magistrate always does or ought to do, but some who are not trained well swear the witness, take oral statements under oath, and then proceed to issue a search warrant. The minister's colleague (Mr. Ralston), a well-trained lawyer who must have had much experience along this line in his younger days, knows that the deposition is the basis of the jurisdiction for issuing a search warrant. If the deposition is bad, the whole thing goes by the board. The same is true of an information in a criminal case; if the information is bad, nothing afterwards can cure the proceeding. If it is defective ab initio it cannot be cured by a hearing later on. It is a long time since I have looked into the matter, but I think that is sound law. You get it so ingrained in your mind that you never forget it. I suggest that the evidence upon which the magistrate issues a search warrant shall be given not only under oath but in writing. I am trying to help the minister improve his bill, not trying to block it at all.

Every complaint shall be for one matter of complaint only, and not for two or more matters of complaint, and every information shall be for one offence only, and not for two or more offences.

It will be a great shock I think to the people to learn that under the guise of war necessity the government is setting aside, when parliament is actually in session, the considered laws of this country. I think the committee will agree that the penalty itself should be severe in cases of this kind, but penalty is one thing and guilt another. The utmost care should be taken, especially in view of the nature of the offence, to give the accused every possible chance to justify his own acts before a fair tribunal, with every opportunity to understand the charge made against him, and to put in his proper defence.
We should not lose sight of the necessity of maintaining the old principle of British justice under which a man is deemed to be innocent until he is proved guilty by an adequate court. We should not depart from this principle by putting too much authority into the hands of a game warden and leaving the accused without any protection whatever. In Ontario particularly, I believe, the principle has generally been observed of keeping the local magistrate in charge of nearly all offences within his jurisdiction and keeping justices of the peace from every judicial position if the magistrate is accessible. I should like to say a

In 1934 there was a very considerable reorganization of the entire arrangements concerning justices of the peace and magistrates -and incidentally constables-in Ontario. It is most important that any dealing with justices of the peace be in line with what Ontario is now doing; and I think other provinces followed the example.
Prior to 1934 in Ontario there was a very large number of local magistrates, men who had their little principalities, with an office in the courthouse, as a rule, in the county town and all the large towns of the province. The number of justices of the peace in Ontario was estimated at 10,000.

speechtext:
Well I swung the axe
with a good deal of satisfaction. Then we proceeded on another basis, that of selecting men of high class in the various communities, the best that could be found, often the clerk of the municipality-men of that type- and making them justices of the peace with authority and a job to be done. Instead of the magistrate hearing first the complaint from the policeman and later the evidence and finally giving the decision, we divided the functions:	first, the policeman laying
the charge; next, the justice of the peace issuing the warrant or summons, preparing the case for trial. Then we divided the province into seventeen great districts, each district having two or three magistrates who travelled around, so that we had itinerant

magistrates instead of local resident magistrates. The effect was tremendous; there was a great improvement in the junior criminal courts of our province. It would be a serious mistake if the dominion government should constitute policemen justices of the peace and reduce the status of the justice of the peace, which during the last six or seven years has been raised to one of real responsibility in the community. That would be a major error.
Three distinct functions are involved here. First there is the function which attaches to the policeman. He is full of suspicion. He has the police mind-and that is the proper mind for a policeman. The justice of the peace is a judicial officer. He decides whether a warrant should or should not issue, whether it should be a summons, or whether any charge at all should be laid. He must know something of the law. It is a mistake to allow the official who prepares the case and does the interlocutory work in the case to make the final decision. You may have a man capable of doing all three, but the public never credit him with the ability. If you are to have justice which is respected by the community you must reserve final decisions to a magistrate who has nothing else to do with the case and is therefore impartial.
I hope this matter will be thoroughly discussed and considered in the light of the experience in my province, supplemented I have no doubt by experience in other provinces, before we take any such step as is suggested.

This is a case of "off again, on again, gone again, Finnegan." The section provides:
The governor in council may as often as occasion requires declare by proclamation that upon and after a day therein named this act 3hall be in force in any province-
The governor in council can undo that and then do it again. I never saw such legislation as this; it is unique. Why is this power required? To-day it is the law, tomorrow it is not, in a given territorial jurisdiction. This kind of legislation is utterly indefensible. The discussion has shown, I think, that this is what I would term ancillary legislation to help the provinces enforce their game laws and collect their revenues. Well. I may be preaching heterodoxy at the moment, but we have never had very much respect for the game laws as such. After all the violation of a game law is not a crime. Those from the province of Quebec who are students of the civil code will recall-and I am in your hands now, Mr. Chairman-things which are called mala in se as distinguished from mala prohibita. In the first case the act is ethically wrong; in the second it is a prohibited act, and some prohibited acts are fantastic. The game laws are enacted on the theory of conservation, of course. The smuggling of game, and smuggling generally to defeat the customs, is merely a prohibited act, and legislation with regard to that is legislation with regard to prohibited acts. How far should this parliament use its power and authority to assist the provinces to enforce the game laws?
There is a principle involved in this legislation. I am not going to oppose the principle; the minister has been satisfied by representations of eight of the nine provinces that they desire this legislation, and so far as I am concerned it is not going to fall on me. I am not going to smuggle any game, and I am not in very great sympathy with those who may do so; but after all there is a principle here in this section. You proclaim it the law to-day and it is not the law to-morrow, by a second proclamation. Think it over; that is all I ask.

speechtext:
Anyone who attempts to practise law is always faced with the problem of knowing what the law is, and the situation is getting worse all the time in this regard. There should be some certainty about the law. If someone comes in and asks, "Well, what is the law in that regard," you should be able, at least in regard to law other than that concerning the war, to look up your revised statutes and the annual revisions of the province and the dominion-and of course if there is any municipal law involved you should get in touch with your municipality-and give a definite answer. But suppose five or six years from now some action is taken under this section. There is a provision here that by proclamation, at any time, this law may be repealed or brought into force again. It may be even repealed and brought into force two or three times in ten years. How in the world is anybody to know what the law is? If you are to have respect for law in this country; if you are to be able to place upon any citizen the onus of being charged with knowledge of the law-because ignorance of the law excuses no one; a man is assumed to know the law-then we must be reasonable with our people and must have the law in such a state that they can be expected to know it. If the law is to be changed by order in council or by proclamation; if it can be brought into force, taken out of force and then brought into force again, how in the world is the citizen or anyone advising the citizen to know what is the law?
The answer may be that you should write Ottawa and find out the law. Is it not getting very far away from the certainty of law and the administration of the law as passed by parliament, if in order to advise a man you

have to get in touch with the government to find out what is the law? I would very strongly advise the minister to eliminate any such provision as this. If people are to obey the law they must know what it is. If we are not to have the law brought into contempt; if we are to have some certainty about it and some respect for it, the people must know what the law is. Otherwise they are going to break it; that cannot be helped. I urge the minister very strongly not to have a provision of this kind in this section. It is bad enough to provide that a section may come into force upon proclamation; then you have to find out if a proclamation has ever been issued. But if you are going to say that a law can be taken out of force by proclamation and then brought back into force in the same way, it seems to me you make it impossible for people to know what is going on.

speechtext: I should like to mention just one or two points which perhaps apply particularly to northern Ontario. Several hon. members have severely criticized the matter of a cumulative fine, but there is something worse so far as the game laws of Ontario are concerned. I do not know that the matter is particularly dealt with in this bill, but in northern Ontario some white poachers have practically mined the game preserves that the Indians have had for so many centuries. Many people suffer in the police magistrates' courts of northern Ontario in this way. A father and son may be caught with twenty beaver pelts and both may be fined in connection with the same pelts. I do not know whether that matter is well defined in the federal law, but certainly it is not in the provincial law. Again you may have two or three people penalized for the same offence. The game warden may bring in the trapper, the buyer and the person in possession of the furs at the time they were seized. I should like the federal department to be thoroughly familiar with this very unfair situation, under which a magistrate may fine three or four persons for the same offence.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of opposing the second reading of this bill. During the course of an earlier debate I made a suggestion to the government with respect to a gift of wheat to our kith and kin across the seas. The suggestion did not meet with very much response from the government, but there have been repercussions from the country with regard to it, and I desire to make a few observations as to an alternative proposal.
My original proposal was the gift of
100,000,000 bushels of wheat out of our great wealth of that commodity. One hundred million bushels of wheat based on an extraction of flour of approximately 80 per cent would result in 80,000,000 bushels of flour, which, at 60 pounds to the bushel, equals
2.400.000	tons of flour. This would leave approximately 20,000,000 bushels, of mill feeds, bran, shorts and middlings, or approximately
600.000	tons. I am suggesting to the government as an alternative that instead of giving wheat we give flour milled in this country. One hundred million bushels of wheat in the form of flour would represent the domestic requirements of the British isles for approximately six months. Would that be too generous a gesture for Canada?
There may be complications in connection with a donation of this kind with regard to the question of maintaining an equity in the matter of sterling exchange. At present prices 100,000,000 bushels of wheat delivered to the Canadian seaboard would represent a donation of approximately $100,000,000. I think that estimate is high, but it would approach that sum of money. The cost of transportation from the Canadian Atlantic seaboard to the United Kingdom would be paid perhaps by the British ministry of shipping. This 100,000,000 bushels of wheat would have to be ground into flour and byproducts. It has been estimated that the
capacity of United Kingdom flour mills has been reduced by over thirty per cent, due to actual damage from bombs, and a further decrease of twenty per cent, making the total efficiency of United Kingdom mills approximately fifty per cent of peace-time capacity, due to intermittent air raids wherein it is necessary to shut down the existing mills.
On the other hand Canadian flour mills, which at the present time are running to not more than sixty per cent capacity, could quite easily take up this grind, particularly since any donation of wheat to Great Britain would result in present flour shipments to Great Britain being displaced to the extent of the wheat donation.
One of the major problems in Canada since the war began has been to provide a supply of feeding stuffs for live stock and dairy interests. The situation is particularly acute in connection with the raising of hogs for bacon. It has been the subject of governmental action in the form of subsidizing the movement of feed grain from western Canada to points in Ontario and, it was suggested, to other points in the eastern provinces. Owing to the lack of ocean space available it does not seem desirable at the present time to ship approximately 600,000 tons of feeding stuffs in the form of wheat to Great Britain. Every effort is being made in that country to produce its own supply of cattle feeds. During the last few months there has been a tendency to decrease the quantity of live stock and its resultant dairy products and import manufactured or semi-processed commodities.
The whole scheme of making a donation to Great Britain, while it may be complicated, in my view has substantial merit. There is a tremendous surplus of Canadian grain in Canada at the present time and with anything like a normal crop in 1941 there certainly will not be sufficient space in the grain elevators and other storage capacities to take care of the crop. A large quantity will have to stay on the farms, and there is bound to be deterioration in quality. A donation of 100,000,000 bushels to Great Britain will not change the picture very much; it will only replace what Great Britain would normally purchase. Unfortunately there is no other large consuming market available for Canadian wheat, as wheat, at the present time.
There is a tremendous possibility behind the whole proposition in the introduction of Canadian spring wheat flour on the United Kingdom market. The domestic consumer in Great Britain is accustomed to blended wheat flour for household use. Canadian spring wheat flour has largely gone to the bakeshops and commercial consumers for the purposes of strengthening soft wheat flours, either grown

locally in Great Britain or imported from other countries. If Canadian flour made from spring wheat could be milled in Canada and shipped in the original containers direct to the householder in Great Britain a very useful purpose would be served in educating the householder to the use of spring wheat flour.
The unit of measure in the milling industry in Canada for flour is the barrel of 196 pounds or multiples thereof. In Great Britain the unit is a sack of 280 pounds or multiples thereof. The normal container shipped from Canada to the United Kingdom is the sack of 140 pounds, or what might be termed a half sack on the British basis of measure. It has been suggested to me that Canadian flour could be shipped in 14-pound cotton bags of which ten are baled in a jute bag. This bag would carry a suitable crest designed and controlled by the dominion government and conveyed by licence to the various mills in Canada which would participate in the movement. The standard would have to be controlled and arrangements would have to be made with the cereals import committee or some British government agency to take delivery at seaboard.
The wheat could be sold to the mills by the Canadian wheat board at a certain price and the flour purchased from the mills f.o.b. seaboard at a price which would make allowance for the conversion costs, plus containers, and deducting an allowance for feedstuffs produced from this wheat. This method would keep the Canadian wheat board balance in shape and the amount paid for the flour at seaboard would represent the actual donation which the Canadian government would make to the British isles.
It is very doubtful if the total amount of the contribution would reach 100,000,000 bushels of wheat. However, there is no apparent reason why many cargoes of Canadian wheat flour should not be moved to Great Britain in the manner I have described, with permanent beneficial results in the reputation which Canadian spring wheat flour would gain in the United Kingdom.
The average ship can carry approximately, as a full cargo, 7,500 tons of flour. It will be realized, therefore, that 100,000,000 bushels of wheat in the form of flour would require in excess of 300 full cargoes, and shipment might be spread over a long period of time. On the other hand, a cargo of 7,500 tons bagged in fourteen pound containers would mean that there would be approximately 1,125,000 bags to be distributed to the consumer; and, as already stated, if this fourteen pound bag were properly labelled as being Canada's contribution to the consumers of Great Britain, the

effect can hardly be estimated. It would not take more than forty cargoes to give full coverage to the entire United Kingdom.
There are many ways in which shipments of this kind could be financed. It could be done by a treasury vote for a full cargo, if the government were disposed, under the War Measures Act or under the war appropriation bill. It might be more desirable to have the flour moving forward in parcel lots along with shipments of munitions and supplies. It might be possible that it could be handled through popular subscription. But this is doubtful with the pressure now on the taxpayer to pay taxes, subscribe for war loans and contribute to different war organizations.
In any event it seems most desirable that, should any movement of this kind be organized, Canada should now ship flour rather than wheat, retain the mill feeds in Canada for domestic consumption, ensure that Canadian spring wheat flour is introduced direct to the householder in Great Britain, arrange for the purchase of containers in Canada much cheaper than now available in Great Britain, retain control of the standard of quality of the flour in Canada, and see that the British consumer realizes that, when a bag of this flour is delivered to him, it is part of Canada's contribution.
There will be other problems in connection with such a distribution in Great Britain. No doubt the flour would have to be shipped to the importers in Great Britain, but the control of the distribution in the United Kingdom would have to be supervised by some representative of the Canadian government to ensure that it would go direct to the consumer.
I offer this in absolute good faith as an alternative, and I hope that the government will give it consideration. I know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made a very important statement the other day with respect to Canada's war contribution, and, measured in terms of dollars and cents, it was immense; I have never attempted to analyse the figures. But it will be recollected that in the last war we did make contributions: provincial governments made donations to the mother country in the form of foodstuffs; and, if I can get the sympathetic ear of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) and the gentlemen who are leading the government on this occasion, I would urge upon them the advisability of giving consideration to a gift of flour to the beleaguered people of Great Britain.

speechtext:
Perhaps this would be
the proper place for me to say a word in answer to what my hon. friend the member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) referred to yesterday afternoon with respect to the relations between the Canadian and British forces and the Canadian and British commands in the United Kingdom.
Let me say that, while stating perhaps the cold legal position, I want it clearly understood that it is the legal position, and that there is no necessity nor do I anticipate that there will be any necessity of our having to invoke it. There has not been the slightest difference of opinion with respect to matters of operations in which the Canadian corps or Canadian forces overseas are or may be engaged. The relationship between the Canadian and British forces and the Canadian staffs and the British staffs could not be more cordial than they have been, and the confidence which exists between them could not, I think, be greater.
Coming to the legal position, as was intimated yesterday afternoon, the Canadian troops are in the United Kingdom under the terms of what is known as the Visiting Forces (British Commonwealth) Act, 1933. That act so far as Canada is concerned is contained in chapter 21 of the statutes of 1933; and the same act, I understand, practically word for word, is on the statute book of the United Kingdom, although the sections are numbered differently.
As hon. members know, the intention of the act is to provide for the relationships existing betwen the so-called home forces, which in the case we are referring to are the United Kingdom forces, and visiting forces, which are the Canadian forces. Two different situations are visualized under the visiting forces act. That is to say, there is one status for the visiting forces, in which they are held to be, as the statute states, serving together with the home forces-that is, the Canadian forces are serving together with the British forces. There is another status in which the Canadian forces are said to be acting in combination with the United Kingdom forces.
Section 6, subsection 4 (a) of that statute provides for the terms of the status when they are serving together. Section 6, subsection 4 (b) provides for the status when they are serving in combination. To make it very brief, the serving together status is more properly adaptable and applicable to the situation where visiting troops are training in the United Kingdom; the status of acting in combination is more adaptable and applicable to the situation where a visiting force
may be called upon to engage in operations along with the United Kingdom forces. The difference in status is this, so far as command is concerned, that when troops are serving together, that is to say more or less on a training basis, they are under separate commands-that is, the home forces are under one command, the Canadian forces are under another command, and there is no common command over them; each is, if I may put it that way, autonomous in connection with its own particular organization and command. When troops are acting in combination, then, as the statute provides, his majesty may provide one officer to act in command of the combined forces.
That is the background of the relationship which exists in the United Kingdom with respect to the Canadian forces. We now come to what has been done in that respect.
The statute provides that the government by order in council may declare that the Canadian forces-I use that term interchangeably with "visiting forces"-shall be deemed to be serving together with the home forces, or the governor in council may declare that the visiting forces shall be acting in combination with the home forces. We have done both. We have passed an order in council, dated April 3, 1940-as a matter of fact it bears the significant and rather intriguing number, 1066-under the War Measures Act. It will be found in volume 2, page 47, of the volume of proclamations and orders in council passed under the War Measures Act. This order in council provides three things: first, that Canadian forces, military and air, in the United Kingdom or the continent of Europe or proceeding from one to the other, serve together with the United Kingdom forces; second, that Canadian forces serving on the continent act in combination upon their embarkation in the United Kingdom for the purpose of proceeding to the continent of Europe.
Third-and this is the important point before us now because we have no forces on the continent of Europe-the order in council provides that those parts of the Canadian forces, military and air, serving in the United Kingdom-'those are our forces which are there at the present time-as may from time to time be detailed for that purpose by the appropriate service authorities as may from time to time be designated by the Minister of National Defence shall act in combination with the United Kingdom forces.
The forces in the United Kingdom are serving together. The Canadian forces are, under the general provision, serving together with the United Kingdom forces and are therefore under separate command.

That third provision of the order in council provides, in effect, that an officer designated by the Minister of National Defence may detail for the purpose of serving in the United Kingdom any portion of those forces to act in combination with the British forces in which case, as I stated a minute ago, by acting in combination they come under a combined command.
Following that through, the Minister of National Defence designated General Mc-Naughton in respect of the Canadian corps; the senior combatant officer at Canadian military headquarters in respect of the troops under his command, and the senior combatant officer in command of any remaining troops in the United Kingdom in respect of forces under his command, to detail the forces or parts of the forces as they might think fit to act in combination with the British forces.
That gave authority to General Mc-Naughton, if he so desired, to detail the Canadian corps, or, as it was then, the first Canadian division, to act in combination with the British forces. He did that. He has detailed the troops of the Canadian corps to act in combination with the troops of the United Kingdom. That is the situation at the present time.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is restricted to serving in Britain?

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That detail is restricted to serving in the United Kingdom.
The senior combatant officer at Canadian military headquarters has not, I understand, detailed the troops under his command to act in combination, because the troops under his command are, generally speaking troops in training, troops at base units, and so forth. There are no other troops in Great Britain except those in the Canadian corps under General McNaughton and those under Canadian military headquarters. That brings the Canadian corps under the command of Sir Allan Brooke, commander in chief of the home forces, by reason of the fact that the Canadian corps has been detailed by General McNaughton to act in combination with the forces of the United Kingdom.
Parallel with that goes this, that under General McNaughton's instructions when he went there, he is directly responsible to the Minister of National Defence and, through the minister, to the Canadian government for the control of the forces under his command. I mention that so that I may indicate what the situation would be with regard to the troops when under Sir Allan Brooke.

The situation, if one were to visualize operations in the United Kingdom, is that Sir Allan Brooke would-I have not any doubt of this-consult with General McNaughton, who is the commander of the Canadian corps and whose troops are acting in combination with the United Kingdom forces under Sir Allan Brooke, in connection with any operation in which the Canadian corps would be committed. I can say that that is done in practice. I can say that it is done on grounds of policy. I can say that it is done also because of the obvious military desirability of a commanding officer in chief consulting with the senior commanding officers of large bodies of troops under his command in connection with any tactical plans which are being made. That is the situation so far as the United Kingdom is concerned.
With regard to the troops going out of England, may I read a paragraph which I have under my hand and which sets out the situation more briefly and succinctly than perhaps I could state it.
As respects any question concerning the employment of the Canadian forces on the continent of Europe or elsewhere, the position is clear, namely, that the decision would rest entirely with the Canadian government. It was in accordance with this principle that the decision was reached last spring to employ Canadian troops in France. Since the change in the situation resulting from the German invasion of France and the low countries, no suggestion of any kind has been made to Canadian military authorities or to the Canadian government that its forces should serve beyond the United Kingdom, except in one instance when the British government requested and the Canadian government approved the dispatch of small detachments of Canadian troops to carry out special work at Gibraltar, of which the house has general information.

The appropriate Canadian service authority has detailed the Canadian corps to serve in combination with the troops of the United Kingdom.
Second, the appropriate Canadian service authority can detail for service within the United Kingdom, but not for service outside, Canadian forces to act in combination. As I have said, General McNaughton has done that in respect of the corps, and General Montague, senior combatant officer at Canadian military headquarters, would have power to detail troops under his command.
Third, the appropriate Canadian service authority cannot authorize the embarkation of Canadian forces from the United Kingdom without the authority of the Minister of National Defence.
Fourth-and this comes by reason of the third clause in the order in council, P.C. 1066-embarkation for the purpose of proceeding to the continent of Europe automatically brings about serving in combination because the order in council contains an express provision. In that case the question as to whether the Canadian troops are serving in combination is not left to the discretion of the general officer commanding, Canadian corps, but assuming that embarkation has taken place by reason of the approval and authorization of the Canadian government, then automatically upon that embarkation
Canadian troops serve in combination with the troops of the United Kingdom on the continent.

Prior to the outbreak of the war, candidates for appointment to commission, in the general list, permanent active air force were required to have a university degree. Shortly after the declaration of the war, this requirement was
[Mr. Green.1
reduced to senior matriculation, or equivalent, which scheme was in effect until the commencement of the joint air training plan. Candidates selected under this scheme were appointed to commissions as pilot officers in the special reserve, subject, of course, to their qualifying as pilots.
It should be noted that prior to the outbreak of war short service appointments for 4 years service in the general list of the auxiliary active air force could be given to candidates with junior matriculation and senior matriculation in mathematics, provided that they were qualified pilots.
When the joint air training plan began, candidates for flying training no longer were commissioned, but were enlisted as A.C. 2's. The educational requirements were also reduced to junior matriculation, or the equivalent.

I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of National Defence a certain matter and ask if he can throw any light upon it. It relates to the recruiting that went on to a considerable extent throughout Canada for the reserve militia, or what is sometimes known as the non-permanent active militia. These young men who enlisted in. the reserve army did so, I think, in all sincerity. Some of them were quite young; some were mere high school students. I think I can say that they enlisted under certain impressions. A good many enlisted with the thought that they were enlisting in a non-permanent force to be used for home defence. Some of them were going to school; some of them had nominal jobs. Their training for the most part took place in the evenings. I refer now to some of the smaller centres where officers were sent down two or three times a week. The young men enjoyed their training and were quite sincere about it.
It appears that a few weeks ago, perhaps a couple of months ago, a circular letter was sent out to these men, I do not know how extensively, whether throughout the entire country or in one section of it, reminding them of their responsibilities and their duties, and the tenor of the letter was to the effect that they might be called up very soon for active militia work. I think one phrase in the letter was that "very short notice may be given," indicating that they should hold themselves in readiness.

Yes. The point I wish to make particularly is this, that in the circular letter reference was made to the Militia
Act. I believe two or three sections were quoted? Section 64, the one to which I wish to refer especially, reads:
The governor in council may place the militia, or any part thereof, on active service anywhere in Canada, and also beyond Canada, for the defence thereof, at any time when it appears advisable so to do by reason of emergency.

Although I do not like to take the time of the committee, I could give a general review of the history respecting export permits. I believe they were first given after section 290 of the Customs Act was amended in 1937, and they were designed to give the government control over the export of munitions, or of raw materials which might enter into the manufacture of munitions. If I remember correctly, under that section exports to Spain were placed under permit.

That was particularly so after this war broke out. Since I left the Department of National Revenue, which has control over the granting of permits, and which has, in fact, an export permits branch, I have lost track of the development of the export permits system. The letter I received came from the Cape Breton Highlanders, who at the present time are stationed at an east coast port.
Before this clause passes, there are a few remarks I wish to make. First, the Minister of National Defence is to be complimented upon the way in which he has handled his department. I notice that the minister takes a note of practically every question, and anything, having to do with his department, which appears to be bothering the mind of any hon. member, he answers to the satisfaction of-at least-the government. At any rate, he brings back an answer, and a member knows exactly where he stands with respect to his question.
My object in rising at this time-and I am sorry that the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Munitions and Supply are not at present in their seats-is this. During the last debate on the main appropriation bill I brought to the attention of the committee

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
two questions which had to do with both the Department of Labour and the Department of Munitions and Supply, and which, in my opinion, are important to the people for whom I attempt to speak.
In the first place, I questioned the minister as to the intentions of the government or the people who claim at the present time ownership of a plate mill located in Sydney, Nova Scotia. To operate that mill would serve two purposes. First, it would relieve unemployment. I know that within the last week the steel plant have on file 1,600 applications for employment. Also it would serve the purpose of augmenting our war effort. I pointed out at that time to the committee that if the government had no intention of doing something about using that mill, and if the people who claim it do not intend to use it, there are others who are seeking to purchase the plant. I received another letter from them. I have not, however, heard anything from the Department of Munitions and Supply as to what they have done about this matter, or whether they have done anything.
It seems to me that it is a waste of time for any hon. member to rise in his place and occupy time in bringing to the attention of the government matters which require to be attended to, if his inquiries are to be relegated to the archives and nothing done about them. The least that any hon. member who brings something to the attention of the government is entitled to is an answer, whether any action is contemplated or not; and the reason why I bring this matter again to the attention of the committee is to inform them that upon this matter, which is of considerable importance, I have not received any answer. The people who were negotiating for the purchase of that plant at Sydney have written me again. The Anglo-French Development Corporation of Montreal, who, on behalf of some clients from overseas, are probing the possibility of that plant being put into production, have written to H. J. Kelly, general manager of Dominion Iron and Steel, of Sydney, on March 13, and they inform me that up to date they have not received the courtesy of a reply from the head of that corporation.
That plant was created during the last war in exactly the same way as industries are being subsidized and financed in this war. The government of this country put four and a half million dollars into that plant. It never went into production; and I understand that, when the war was over, the federal government was sued for breach of contract and considerably more money was

extracted from the Canadian taxpayer. If that plant has been damaged to a point where it will cost a substantial sum of money to put it back into production, it is the responsibility of the federal government to find out exactly what the situation is. In my opinion, the people who claim the plant do not own it. If others seek to purchase it, and it will serve the purpose of augmenting our war effort as well as reducing unemplo3rment in that section, it is the responsibility of the Minister of Munitions and Supply at least to tell the committee what he has done about a matter of that importance. The people in our locality are interested in the question; I know that this Montreal corporation is also interested in it; and if H. J. Kelly is not concerned about answering correspondence from that corporation, it seems to me that some one should do something about it.
Another matter, which I brought to the attention of the Minister of Labour, and with regard to which I have received no answer, is the situation which exists at Hamilton, Ontario, where some forty ex-service men who were employed as shell inspectors by the Canada Car company, which is engaged in war production at the present time, were replaced by girls at a lower rate of wages and, as far as my information goes, are still unemployed.

He said that they did, and that there may be responsibility for taking care of Canadian citizens who are employed in this British production organization. This was some time ago. I have not received any reply from the minister as to what has been done. Is it the intention of the government or of the Department of Labour to ensure that some employment is obtained for the men who are on the street? Is it the policy of the government to create more unemployment as far as the males of this country are concerned, with particular reference to the men who went through the last war, by replacing them with girls, because their labour can be got cheaper? If that is the policy, then we should know it.

Had either of the ministers written me a note, I would know at least where I stand. When I bring up a matter here in this chamber, it is not for fun. I like to have an answer. I ask for replies to both these questions: What is the intention of the Minister of Labour with respect to this situation at Hamilton? What is the intention of the Minister of Munitions and Supply with respect to that plate mill at Sydney, Nova Scotia? It can be used. People are trying to purchase it. The government have an equity in it. The taxpayers of Canada have practically paid for it. The people who claim it at the present time and who, according to my information, have denuded it, stripped it of its inner workings and transferred them elsewhere, are making no use of it, and I can understand why. There is no intention on the part of the people engaged in the manufacture of steel in Canada to-day to set up competition among themselves; there is no intention of expanding that industry beyond what it is at the present time. If this is a demonstration to the Canadian people of how an industry created by the taxpayers is to be handled in the aftermath of this war, then drastic changes must take place; and the attitude of this government, if they are going to allow a plant of this kind to lie idle when it might be made use of, must be taken as an indication of what their attitude will 'be with respect to government-assisted industries after the war.

speechtext: I had a question which I wished to direct to the Minister of Mines and Resources or to the Secretary of State. Possibly, since they are not at present in the chamber, the Minister of Finance can give me the information I require. I understand that last summer, after the fall of France and Belgium, about 4.000 aliens were transferred from Great Britain to Canada, and that, while many of these people were enemies of Hitler, the fact that they were aliens was a sufficient reason for moving them from Great Britain. I understand that some have been sent to the United States and others have been returned to Great Britain. There are in Canada quite a number of them who, I believe, are as bitterly opposed to Hitler and Mussolini as we are. I wonder whether some of those who are, trained technicians might not find some employment in some of our wTar industries in Canada. I understand there are a number of university graduates and undergraduates who are interned, and as matters now stand, it is next to impossible, I believe, for these interned persons to be given permission to stay in Canada, even if it is proved that they are very much opposed to Hitler and our enemies. What is the possibility of some of these people being permitted to make a contribution in Canada towards the defeat of our common enemy?

On this or some other section I wanted to give the committee information in reply to some questions. The hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Hazen) asked some questions with regard to fires which had occurred and the safeguards observed in connection with the building and use of military establishments. I think it is due to the officers of the department that this should be on record, and I give my hon. friend and the committee the information I have from the quartermaster-general.
One question was whether instructions were given to officers to observe the by-laws of municipalities for preventing fires. The answer is that no recent instructions have been issued in the exact terms the hon. member used; but under standing instructions for engineer sendees in Canada, district engineer officers follow local and fire underwriters' requirements as far as practicable. Municipal, provincial and dominion fire marshals are encouraged to inspect the properties and report. Definite instructions are issued regarding precautionary measures for preventing fires.
The hon. member spoke of certain fires at Fredericton, Saint John and Yarmouth. The cause of the Fredericton fire has not yet been established. There is suspicion of incendiarism. The O'Regan fire was caused by carelessness of an individual, and was not due to the heating and lighting system. It was apparently started by a cigarette thrown into floor-sweepings. A report of the proceedings at the court of inquiry has not yet been received. The Yarmouth fire was apparently caused by the explosion of a heating stove while the building was unoccupied.

The hon. member brought to my attention a report of January 16 by Colonel E. J. Mooney, building inspector, made to the Saint John city council, stating that the defence department were doing work without building permits. He said, I think, that Colonel Mooney spoke to Major Blake, district engineer officer, who informed him that the engineers could design and build to their own ideas and that the local civic authorities had no jurisdiction. Major Blake, district engineer officer at military district No. 7. states definitely that he never was approached by Colonel Mooney, and that Colonel Mooney has never spoken to him regarding building permits or inspection of military buildings.
The hon. member said also that there were infractions with regard to fire prevention safeguards; he spoke of furnaces in the exhibition building being placed on thin concrete slabs on top of wood floors. He spoke of stovepipes being run through wood partitions without proper insulation, and said the fire department had to be called to extinguish fires in these buildings. He said that in the exhibition buildings there were five stoves with chimneys all connected with seven-inch jointed stovepipe running through fibre board false ceiling and floor, and then to the roof, the chimney without any sort of insulation; that it must have been red-hot at times, and that this would set fire to the dust.
The information I got from the quartermaster-general is that as far as the furnaces are concerned, they were placed on four-inch hollow tile and under that there is, not what I would call a thin concrete slab, but a four-inch concrete slab. The pipes from these furnaces were carried to brick chimneys which were specially built; there were, at various points in the building, seven or eight small stoves from which stovepipes had to be carried up through the roof. All pipes had protective arrangements and all were inspected by the fire underwriters1 association representative.
The hon. member said also that the fire underwriters had looked into the situation and made two reports, the first showing that there were great fire hazards, which had been corrected. The second report said that not only had the former hazards been replaced but greatly increased. He spoke of the exhibition building being destroyed and one man having lost his life.
The reply is that the exhibition buildings at Saint John were inspected by a representative of the fire underwriters' association in company with Major Blake in the early winter of 1939-40, and that all suggestions made by the representative were carried out. The buildings were again inspected by the same representative later, and he expressed

himself as completely satisfied that all reasonable precautions were taken. No report has ever been made to military district No. 7 by the fire underwriters' association. It is not known how the unfortunate man who lost his life came to be in the building.
Then my hon. friend spoke of the temporary huts, stating his information was that they were constructed of light inflammable wood with pitch roof, false fibreboard ceilings, with jointed stovepipes running up through to peak, with no insulation whatever.
As my hon. friend knows, the war-time hutments must necessarily be of wood and of the cheapest possible construction. Efforts have been directed against the occurrence of fires. All buildings are given a plentiful supply of fire-extinguishers, fire-buckets and so on, and in addition a good system of outside hydrants is provided in all camps. All stovepipes are protected by standard equipment where they pass through ceilings to the roof. We have had several thousand similar huts in Canada, and not had one of these destroyed by fire from the stovepipes, indicating that the stovepipe protection is adequate.
Then the hon. member asked whether the fires had been investigated and who investigated them. All fires, including those referred to by the hon. member, are investigated by a court of inquiry. The proceedings of the courts of inquiry are sent to national defence headquarters for review. Proceedings in connection with the exhibition fire at Saint John have not yet been received, and consequently no action has yet been taken. In any event where evidence indicates that disciplinary action should be taken, this action is taken by the adjutant-general.

One or two questions were asked which I might answer at this time. In the first place the hon. member for Vancouver South, who, unfortunately, is not in the chamber at the moment, asked a question respecting age limits. I should like to give the committee the information I got in connection with the matter about which he spoke this afternoon, namely, the enlistment in Vancouver of men under nineteen years of age. I believe the facts are as I suggested to him, namely, that the enlistments are being made, not in mobile units, which were the units mentioned in the order to which I referred this afternoon, but, as I suggested, in coast defence units. The information I have is that we telephoned military district No. 11 this afternoon to ascertain the reason for the press announcement by Colonel Goodman, and were informed that recruits between the ages of eighteen and nineteen were being enlisted, but only for coast defence units such as artillery, signals, and so on, and not for units of the mobile force, referred to in routine order 138-39.
Military district No. 11 also stated that these young men between eighteen and nineteen were definitely recruited for home service in coast defence units, although on reaching the age of nineteen they would be given an opportunity of volunteering as reinforcements for overseas service. In the meantime they are replacing, in the coast defence units, personnel of nineteen years and over who have volunteered for service overseas.

I have tried for the last two and a half weeks to get definite statistical information to support the argument I am now making. I have been unable to get sufficient to cover all the ground, but I think most of what I shall say is a matter of common observation. Land in western Canada is cheaper than similar land in Ontario and Quebec, adjacent to centres of population. Second, lands adjacent to cities in eastern Canada offer more hazards to aviation, and they must be cleared of the natural growth thereon in the form of trees. Farms in Ontario are for the most part one hundred acre farms divided into three or four fields; so it is not an unfair assumption, but one which I think will be borne out by the statistics when they are produced, that the cost of levelling and clearing airfields in eastern Canada is higher than in western Canada. subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Would the
Minister of National Defence for Naval Services make a supplementary statement respecting the construction of ships in Nova Scotia? I am referring more particularly to the construction of wooden ships. The statement he made in the house a few weeks ago with regard to this matter was a great disappointment to the people of Nova Scotia. The people in that province feel that the capacity of the shipyards of Nova Scotia has not been used even to a fraction of their possible use in the building of wooden ships, ships which could carry cargo, powered with diesel engines and capable of keeping up with the average convoy. They could do coastal work and thereby release steel ships to be used in the transatlantic service.
The minister's statement was supported and confirmed by the premier of Nova Scotia who took credit for obtaining large shipbuilding orders for Nova Scotia. It was stated by the premier that the Nova Scotia yards had been given an opportunity to build ships, but that they refused. These statements are not satisfactory to the people of Nova Scotia.
and are a disappointment to Canadians as a whole. I do not believe we are doing justice to Lord Beaverbrook and to the British people who have made an appeal to people the world over for ships. The minister said that the demand for ships was first in war necessities, even coming ahead of the building of aeroplanes. I feel that much more could and should be done by the government in assisting, encouraging and, if necessary, compelling the people of Nova Scotia to build ships. This is a supplementary appropriation, and I should like to have a supplementary statement from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am not just sure what information the hon. member for Cumberland requires. In the first place the business of building cargo ships or, in fact, the building of ships of war, is not one administered by the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. All these matters are dealt with by the Department of Munitions and Supply.
I would, however, say to the hon. member that, so far as I know, up to the present time no assistance has been given to any shipyard in this country. In my view that point ought to be cleared up at once. There are some people in certain parts of the country who seem to think that because the government is assisting certain manufacturers to set up industries, which are essentially and only war industries, therefore the government should assist any industry. For example, let us consider the building of corvettes. To the extent to which we were asked to build them in this country, the building of corvettes could be taken care of without any difficulty whatever in existing Canadian shipyards. I ask the hon. member, and any other member in the committee, if it would be reasonable to expect the government of Canada to establish new shipyards for the building of corvettes when there were in Canada plenty of yards which could handle all the corvettes we want. It would be utterly unreasonable, I suggest, to establish such yards. The fact that a man who is asked to manufacture munitions or something of that kind-commodities the use of which will vanish at the end of the war-is given some assistance by the government is, I suggest, no reason whatever why we should believe that everything manufactured for war should be subsidized by the government. We had some twenty yards in Canada capable of building corvettes, and capable of building certain other ships required for war purposes.
The question which I suggest people ought to ask themselves before they begin saying that the government should force Nova Scotia shipbuilders or any other shipbuilders into a
2074	COMMONS
Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
programme of plant expansion is whether existing plants have been taxed beyond their capacity. Until that time arrives, I do not think it is the function of government-this or any other government-to begin to subsidize or to bonus shipyards and shipbuilding.
The other night, in the absence of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, I made a statement respecting the building of wooden cargo ships. My hon. friend now asks me to amplify that statement. I can say to him that the opinion of certain British shipping experts is that a ship of even 4,700 tons, the size of ship the building of which was considered in this country a short time ago, is practically too small to-day for convoy work. I do not say there are not some ships of a tonnage less than 4,700 plying the seas; as a matter of fact, there are a few. But these men are thinking of building ships, and their advice to this country is, if you are going to build ships, do not build a ship as small as 4,700 tons. That ship has to go in convoy; it has to be cared for in the same way as if it were a ship of 10,000 tons. It is not so economical, ton for ton, as a 10,000 tonner, and all in all it is not wise to undertake the building of ships of this size.
My hon. friend knows veiy well that when you speak of wooden ships and when you speak of 4,700 ton ships, you are referring to two totally different things. You cannot build, a wooden ship of that size. While it has been suggested, I believe, that there are in Nova Scotia fifty yards which can undertake the building of cargo ships, in my opinion a statement of that kind is in need of the most drastic revision.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It all
depends upon what the minister means by "cargo ships."

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am saying to my hon. friend that the advice of the British authorities who have come to this country-and I would suppose that theirs is the best advice in the world when it comes to shipping of any sort, mercantile ships or warships-is, that it is unwise to talk of convoys across the Atlantic composed of ships even of 4,700 tons; and I say that when you get to that tonnage, you are entirely out of the wooden ship class.
What other yards are there in Nova Scotia capable of building steel ships? The shipyards at Halifax can do so, but they are engaged at the moment in other duties which are regarded as of even greater importance. They have been asked to undertake and are undertaking repair work. I do not know of

any other shipyards equipped to build steel ships. There is no question that such shipyards could be established.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Were not ships of substantial tonnage built there on a large scale during the last war? I do not remember how big the ships were, but I know they did construct steel ships.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
During the last war they built steel ships at New Glasgow; they built them also at Halifax, and of as great a tonnage as 9,500. That could be done again.; but the question is, is this government called upon now to establish a shipyard at, we will say, New Glasgow, where there is no yard at the present time, while there are yards at British Columbia, on the river St. Lawrence and on the great lakes which are capable of building these ships? That is the whole question. If this country desires this government to go into the business of establishing yards in competition with those existing yards, which so far as I know are capable of taking care of all the business which offers at the present time-if the people want the government to subsidize yards in competition with these existing yards, that is another story. But if my hon. friend can tell me of any yard in Nova Scotia which is capable to-day of building steel ships for cargo purposes-and that is the only type which can be considered for transatlantic purposes-I would be glad to have the name of that yard. If my hon. friend can nanm me any yard in Nova Scotia which is capable of building ships for war purposes and has not been given an opportunity of bidding on these ships, I should like to have its name. I can tell him that, when it came to the construction of wooden ships, I hoped that a great number of them would be built in Nova Scotia. I knew that British Columbia and other provinces had been building steel ships, because they had yards equipped for the purpose. Steel ships have been built on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence, but none had been built in Nova Scotia. As I have said, the only yard in that province which is capable of doing that work was assigned to other essential war work. I had hoped, however, that a great many wooden ships would be built in Nova Scotia, as some measure of compensation for the contracts for steel ships which had gone elsewhere.
There were twenty-four Fail-miles to be built. They were wooden ships, 112 feet long, costing not more than $100,000 each for the hull. I believe that last fall the Department of Munitions and Supply was prepared to give contracts for eighteen or twenty of these ships

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
to Nova Scotia if the builders in that province were prepared to take them. The department sent down the director of shipbuilding to examine the yards and see whether they were capable of undertaking this work. He returned and made a report in which he listed, I believe, some six, or perhaps it was as many as ten, Nova Scotia yards which could do the work. Bids were asked for, but only three Nova Scotia yards bid on these ships; and this is the province which is the home of wooden shipbuilding in Canada. Of these three bidders, only one was at all within the range of the bids offered by builders in Ontario, on the St. Lawrence and in British Columbia.
So amazed was I at the discrepancy in prices that I suggested to the Minister of Munitions and Supply and to the director of shipbuilding that Nova Scotia builders must have made some mistake, that presumably they had misunderstood the specifications, and that they should be given another opportunity. That opportunity was given them; they bid a second time, and again, only one man was at all within the range. There were bidders in British Columbia whose bids were S25.000 below the second and third Nova Scotia bids on a job which was worth something less than $100,000. Does my hon. friend or does any sane person in this country contend that we should accept those bids from Nova Scotia and award contracts on that basis? As a matter of fact, we had to ask the one bidder at Weymouth to undertake two ships instead of one. The result is that, of the twenty-four Fairmiles, two only are being built in Nova Scotia.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They are patrol vessels. We asked for bids for wooden mine-sweepers, and again I may say that I hoped that most of them might be built in Nova Scotia. subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: For what reason?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
For one reason or another. One had difficulty in getting capital. Another said that the specifications were too difficult. The result is that only six of these ten boats are being built in Nova Scotia, and the other four are being built on the St. Lawrence or on the lakes. That is the story with regard to the minesweepers.
What more could be done than was done by this government so far as the building of wooden ships is concerned? I stated the other night that the government of Nova Scotia had called a meeting of all the shipbuilders in that province. I think two meetings were held, and they got a delegation of shipbuilders to come to Ottawa. They got the best naval architect in Nova Scotia, Mr. Rowe, the designer of the great ship Bluenose, to accompany them as a technical expert and had with them also a minister of the Nova Scotia government. They interviewed representatives of the Department of Munitions and Supply and they interviewed me, and everything was done that could possibly be done to stimulate the development of the wooden shipbuilding industry in Nova Scotia. But for one reason or another the situation is as I have stated. What the full reasons are I do not know. It may be as the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley)

suggested, that it was lack of capital. There may have been difficulty in understanding the specifications. It may have been that the wood which they had to use in these ships was foreign wood that had to be imported.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

If my hon. friend can suggest any other definite thing that can be done, I shall be glad to discuss it with my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply to see what can be done, but I do not think it is of any use to make general observations like "every shipyard should be busy and all Nova Scotia shipyards should be working.'' when in some respects the yards themselves have not taken full advantage of the opportunities that offered.
