If that is the requirement, Mr. Chairman, and the building of ships is as urgent as we know it is-there is no question about that- I say that the government has not put forth a full effort in obtaining ships from Nova Scotia. The Minister of National Defence for Naval Services has criticized the people of Nova Scotia and the shipyards of that province because they' have not built ships of foreign wood. There is a feeling among the shipbuilders of Nova Scotia, in the shipyards, that this government does not want them to build ships; otherwise specifications would be drawn up calling for materials that are native to Nova Scotia, such materials as Nova Scotians have been using in years long gone by in the building of ships that were able to weather the storms of every ocean. The shipbuilders of Nova Scotia, however, are now being asked to build ships from foreign woods, southern woods such as mahogany and teak, and even from British Columbia, rather than from woods native to the province. If the government were doing its full part in encouraging the people of Nova Scotia to build ships such as they are capable of building, and as I believe they wish to build in their desire to discharge their patriotic duty, then the government, in justice to Nova Scotia, would draw up specifications calling for materials which are available in that province and out of which the shipbuilders have been constructing ships for a century or more.
I believe that this is due the province of Nova Scotia. Money has been available without stint for many other forms of war work, and war materials. There is no question about money, so far as the members of this house are concerned, if that money is to be used for supplying the necessities of war. There is no question in the minds of members of this house about the supplying of money if the government asks for it for the purpose
Supplementary

War Appropriation Bill
of building ships in Nova Scotia or anywhere else. As one hon. member has already said, it is not so much a question of money as it is a question of ships. This parliament and the people of Canada will provide the money if the government will do their part and get every shipyard busy which is capable of building ships, whether in Nova Scotia or in any other part of Canada. I say to the government: Listen to the call of Beaverbrook; listen to the call of every one who is familiar with the needs of our empire at this time and get ships built.
In my opinion, we should go further in Nova Scotia. A special appropriation should be made in order that steel plates might be rolled in that province. The capacity of the steel mills should be increased to enable us to produce materials out of which steel ships can be built, not only for the war but for use after the war, when the need will be great. The difficulty in Nova Scotia in much of its war work-and there is only a limited amount compared with what is being done in other parts of Canada-is that most of it will cease on the termination of the war and we shall have no new industries. I contend that a steel shipbuilding yard should be established in Nova Scotia. It should be started without a day's delay, and plates should be rolled in that province to enable us to do our part in the war and after. We should be put in the position of building ships after the war to replace the enormous tonnage that is being sunk every week.
I for one, coming from Nova Scotia, and speaking, I believe, for the people of that province, am not satisfied with the efforts of the government and the results they have obtained with respect to shipbuilding in that province.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The fact of the matter is that the government has no national shipbuilding policy. I urged this on a previous occasion at great length. The government should take a long-term view of the question of establishing in Canada a national shipbuilding policy, so that we might, in a degree at least, recover our position as a great shipping country. I received no response from the Minister of Munitions and Supply except a detail later on of what had been done with respect to the building of these small war vessels. That is not the point of view the Canadian people are asking this government to take at the moment. It is all right to buy yachts in a hurry, to build corvettes for patrol purposes; it is all right to build mine-sweepers. But what we on this side of the house are urging, and what the people of Nova Scotia are urging, is a

little vision on the part of the government on the question of a great national policy; that is to say, the establishment of a steel shipbuilding industry in Canada on the Atlantic coast.
Talk about the St. Lawrence yards! There are two yards in the lower stretches of the St. Lawrence for the building of 10,000-ton ships, but you could not bring 10,000-ton ships down from lake ports. Why in the world this government, with all the money that we have voted to them so freely, cannot have a little vision and establish a national shipbuilding programme in this country, I cannot understand. We can find money for everything else.
We can bonus wheat and summer-fallowing and all that. But here is something that would be a post-war industry in Nova Scotia. Why should it not be established at Sydney? Why should it not be established at New Glasgow? The minister says there is no yard there now. I tell him, the yard was there in the last war and could be reassembled at not very great cost. The people of Nova Scotia demonstrated in the last war that they could build steel ships of very large capacity. This can be done again, and I ask the minister to review' the whole position in the interests of Nova Scotia and of the maritime provinces. Let us get back something of the position we once occupied in this country in relation to the sea. To take the attitude that the minister has taken with respect to Nova Scotia shipbuilding is to admit defeat before you start. I do not think the minister is a defeatist, but at the moment he is concentrating his mind especially on the immediate necessities of the occasion. I visualize something a great deal bigger than that. I wish the minister had the vision of the late William Pugsley who started the whole idea of building steel ships in Canada.

Some day, if we have vision and energy enough, we shall have in the maritimes again a great shipbuilding industry such as that which put Nova Scotia on the map. It can be done. The people of the maritime provinces are being given by time and circumstance one last opportunity to come back. And they can do it. We have not exported all the mentality for which we were famous in days gone by. It is true we supplied the banks and the prominent pulpits in Canada, and many other high positions, with the best men they ever had in those positions, but we still have a good many left. speechtext:
Up to the present time we have been discussing this bill in terms of money and aeroplanes and shipbuilding and so on. In the few minutes I am going to take up I am going to refer to the human element. In my constituency of Three Rivers is located a machine gun training centre. The men who compose that company or regiment came from different parts of Canada. I understand that quite a number of them came from Ontario, some from the maritime provinces and some from my own province. When men misconduct themselves or do not behave properly, we are always ready to find fault; but when men conduct themselves as men should, we pass it by and do not refer to it. I wish to commend the conduct of those men in that machine gun training centre in my county and say that they are an honour to their fathers and mothers and to the government, and. I should say, a source of great satisfaction to the Minister of National Defence. During the time those men have been in our
city I am happy to say there has not been a single complaint by the police department or any citizen with regard to their conduct when they come down to visit the city. I think we should refer to the men and their conduct more often than we do. There are men located all through this country giving their time for very little money, and when we have anything good to say about them we should say it. It is my pleasure to-night to be able to say this about these men.
I wish also to give credit to the commanding officer, Colonel D. S. Forbes, late of McGill university. Montreal. Much of the credit is due to Colonel Forbes. According to my judgment he is a human being, one whom the uniform has not spoiled. He understands his men and does everything he can to set them a good example.
While I am on this subject I wish to refer to another matter. That machine gun training centre is located, I believe, at one of the best locations that can be found anywhere in Canada. It is a splendid site on a hill above the city; the soil is sandy, and in 1938 there was built in these exhibition grounds new buildings at a cost of a million dollars. There is a splendid swimming pool there; I do not think there is the like of it in Canada, or any better. There is a splendid baseball field and excellent grounds. The city of Three Rivers has rented that property to the defence department for a dollar a year for the duration of the war.
In conclusion, the city of Three Rivers will always be ready to receive men from different parts of Canada who will conduct themselves like the men who are there to-day.

There is something in what he said about our Vision and Energy. We must get back to material things and be practical if we want to succeed in industry.
It has been my privilege during the last few weeks to talk several times with the Minister of Munitions and Supply about shipbuilding in Nova Scotia and on Canada's eastern coast. I believe he is alive to the situation; in fact, I think at this moment his technical men are

I have no doubt there was difficulty, due to some extent to the red tape that always prevails in some measure in connection with government business. It must be remembered also that some yards were held up because their financial position did not justify giving them contracts under existing conditions. It seems to me these yards could and should have been helped. I understand efforts have been made to get the banks to help, and I believe progress has been made in that regard. I understand that in my hon. friend's county of Cumberland, a couple of mine-sweepers are being built. Perhaps with a review of the situation, with a settling of the difficulties as between the ideas of the shipbuilders and those of the technical men, who are not always right, we may arrive at some common understanding which will permit of the construction of wooden ships of a size which will allow them to be used for certain war activities, as well as ships for the usual trade of the country.
We have heard much about these Fairmile boats. We were told they were more expensive to build in Nova Scotia than in other parts of Canada. The Fairmile boat is of two-ply mahogany with canvas in between, and that, type of construction was an innovation in Nova Scotia. These are high-powered boats formerly built on the great lakes for sportsmen, and when one undertakes the construction of new types of boats, it is pretty hard to get men into such a hazardous business, where there is a great deal of depreciation in connection with the installation of equipment which, after the war will be a total loss. These men must consider the matter very carefully. However, one builder, and he is a good one, gave a tender in line with other parts of Canada.
I do not think we should make shipbuilding in any part of this country a matter of political preferment, but shipbuilding is natural to Nova Scotia. So far as I am concerned, I am here to do what I can to promote shipbuilding on

the coast. I know that the ministers and officers of this government have gone a long way in trying to meet the situation that now exists, but if we are going to have shipbuilding carried on in Nova Scotia, somebody must wake up. I hope this discussion may help to bring that about.

speechtext: To-night we have heard a strange principle enunciated by a minister of the crown. When he is asked why we do not mobilize an industry in order that it may produce, he says we do not intend to gestapo people into producing something if they do not want to produce it.

Here we have an abundance of it, and the only thing lacking is that bridge of ships for which Beaverbrook is calling, for which Churchill has been calling and for which even the President of the United States has been making a heroic plea. speechtext:
I
say that my hon. friend and his associates were foremost in this country, and have been for many years, in opposing defence estimates of one kind or another. If my hon. friend had had his way, we would not have a Canadian ship on the sea to-day. His party sat in this house in 1939 and said that we should not send a single man overseas. That was their idea of loyalty. I am telling him now that if he had had his way, there would not be a single man in the Canadian navy, and there would not be a single ship on the sea, because when a man enters the Royal Canadian Navy he volunteers to do service in any part of the world where duty calls him. This is the hon. gentleman who now comes to this house and attempts to say that I would be better as a lawyer than as a minister of the navy. I will tell my hon. friend that if he cannot make a better show in his argument than he made to-night, then he had better turn to some other pursuit, and stay there.
It has been suggested by the leader of the opposition and by the hon. member for Cumberland that the attitude I have adopted with regard to Nova Scotia shipbuilding is a defeatist attitude. That phrase was coined or used, I believe, by a newspaper in Halifax whose editorials lately on the question of shipbuilding have been remarkable for what they did not contain. They have been referring to the attitude of people who faced the facts and told the facts to the people of Nova Scotia, and have described that attitude as defeatist. I have done as much for Nova Scotia as most men who have spent a similar number of years in public life. There has never been a time in the years I sat in the legislature of Nova Scotia when I did not devote every energy I had to the development of the industry of that province. But I never told the people of Nova Scotia at any time, and I am not going to tell them to-day from this chamber, things which are not so. I am not going to tell the people of Nova Scotia that the blame is with the Department of Munitions and Supply, or that it is due to some specification or to some kind of wood which is used in the ships, when I know that is not the real reason.
The leader of the opposition referred to the spirit of the people of the maritimes, and expressed the hope that it might be revived. I have wondered whether the spirit of Nova Scotian builders and shipping interests is what it was three quarters of a century ago. I doubt very much whether the grandfathers of these men, the old fellows who were building ships in the fifties and sixties and seventies of the last century, would have taken second
place to any province or any country in the world when it came to building ships cheaply, efficiently and speedily. Nova Scotia in the middle of the last century had a greater tonnage on the seas of the world, per capita, than any other country. Its ships were on every sea; its captains and its sailors were known in every port. But I doubt whether some of the shipbuilders of to-day have the spirit of their fathers; and when people, in this chamber or in the press of this country, lay the blame for the non-existence of shipbuilding in that province on factors which have very little to do with the situation, I think it is time that somebody spoke out and gave the real facts.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What is wrong with the builders?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg mentioned that the specifications for the Fairmile boats and the mine-sweepers were British specifications. That is absolutely true. Some of these boats were destined for the Royal Navy, and we had no other course than to comply with those specifications. If they wanted us to build boats of silver we should have to try to do it, or throw up the sponge. They wanted mahogany; they wanted teak, and there is no country in the world which can build warships of any kind as well as the people of Britain can do it. When they asked us for Fairmiles with mahogany decks or planks and with teakwood here or there, there was nothing for us to do but to accept their specifications and build ships in accordance with those specifications.
I do not know whether the leader of the opposition is suggesting the establishment in this country of a government mercantile marine. If he is, that is a suggestion which perhaps	is worth	considering.But I say again, so far as ships for the Royal Canadian Navy are concerned, ships of war,	there is	no lack of	capacity	in
Canadian yards.
So far as cargo ships are concerned, although	I should	prefer the	Minister	ofMunitions and Supply to make this statement, because I am altogether out of my own department. I know of no shortage in that regard; I know of no shipyard in Canada	which is	turning away work;	I
know of no danger of having our existing yards overburdened. Under these circumstances the point upon which I should like the leader of the opposition to elaborate is whether he believes that the government should now undertake, in addition to all the work which is being given to the shipyards of this country, the establishment of

a Canadian mercantile marine, and whether, for that purpose, it should establish government shipyards. If that is what he means, it is, as I say, a suggestion perhaps worthy of some consideration. But up to the moment, whether in respect of cargo ships or ships of war, I am aware of no lack of capacity in Canadian yards, and certainly there is no lack of willingness or zeal on the part of Canadian builders to undertake any task which the government, or, indeed, any private individual, sets before them in furtherance of this country's war effort.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I accept without reserve the statement of the minister that, so far as the limited programme of shipbuilding which the Department of Munitions and Supply have instituted, is concerned, there is no lack of capacity in Canada. But the Minister of Munitions and Supply, when we discussed this matter on an earlier occasion, and he was pressed to expand the programme of shipbuilding in Canada, put the position on an entirely different basis. What he said was that there were no skilled workmen in Canada. It was not a question of capacity but a question of ability to perform upon which he made his defence for not doing more than we were asking him to do. I suggest that the two stories do not jibe: I am, going to leave it there.
There is involved in this a larger question to which the minister adverted just before he resumed his seat. I want the ministry to explore all possible avenues of building up in Canada a commercial shipbuilding industry. It has started on the Pacific coast; it has not flourished on the Atlantic coast. Now, when ships are needed, is the opportunity to get this programme going on a commercial basis. Whether it shall be done as a government-owned, a government-operated or a privately initiated enterprise, is a matter for grave consideration. I do not mind telling the minister that, so far as I am concerned,
I would prefer, after the matter is gone into thoroughly and given the best consideration that the authorities and the technical men can give it, as to ways and means, that the decision should be that it should not be a government-owned or a government-operated project. What I visualize is a commercial enterprise which may be assisted by the government, in the establishment of yards, and, in the construction of a plate mill on the Atlantic coast. It is not beyond our powers to do this, and it should be started now if we as a nation are to reap any of the benefits of it and to give Great Britain the assistance which an all-out war effort on the part of this country requires, and

for which our people are calling in accents louder than I can use. That is what I am asking the ministry to visualize and to consider. We will support them in any well-thought-out enterprise.
What can be done on the Pacific coast with respect to steel shipbuilding surely can be done in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I do not believe that all the initiative has as yet gone out of Nova Scotia. I learn that some of our friends in Nova Scotia find it difficult to get this government interested in Nova Scotia enterprise, and I can tell the minister of a specific case. It took months to convince the Department of Munitions and Supply that munitions could be made at Trenton, in the county of Pictou. I know that the manager of the Trenton plant was in Ottawa and spent days and weeks in trying to get an order. He never did get an order from this government, but he got one from the department for the account of the British government. He had infinite trouble in getting it. I do not know the reason, and I am not going to allocate any blame. There may have been a very good reason why he could not get an order for munitions for the plants in Pictou county, but he himself told me of the difficulties and discouragements which he had encountered. Finally he did get an order, for the account of the British government, made, of course, through the single purchasing channel. I approve that principle, because I do not think it would be wise to have two competing agencies in Canada for this type of work; the principle w'hich has been set up by the Minister of Munitions and Supply and his advisers is a sound one; but there has been some difficulty-I will not say resistance-in the working out of the principle.
The only reason why I rose again was that the minister rather invited me to give my opinions with respect to the question of commercial shipbuilding. That is the one I am interested in. I do not think for one minute that with the lack of technical men in Canada we can hope during this war-and I do not think we shall want to do it after this war- to build naval vessels of any size and power that cannot be far better built in Britain than we could do it here even in times of peace.
Somebody may say: They can build cargo ships over there better than we can build them in Canada in times of peace. That may be true. The first cost of establishing a shipbuilding enterprise in Canada will be heavy. It will cost us more here, I have no doubt; but I do not think it will be 100 per cent more, as the Minister of Munitions and Supply suggested the other day. I believe that, as time goes on, and we understand things better,

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
the costs will be reduced. There is an opportunity, if we have the vision as a people, as a government, and as a parliament, and if we make an appeal to the commercial enterprise of our citizenship, to establish in the provinces by the sea a commercial shipbuilding enterprise. That is what I invite the minister and liis colleagues to give their attention to from now on so far as it is possible for them to do so. I want to see it started now in order that we may have a post-war industry that may be a continuing industry, so that Canada will get back on the map once more as a seafaring country as we were in days gone by. It is not beyond the realm of possibility at all. It is, on the contrary, well within the range of possibility. All we need is vision and energy and the spirit to go ahead and do it. Once we get going, we can build ships as cheaply as they can build them in the United States. Let me say to the minister that "without vision the people perish." We must have a little more vision in the maritime provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: And private enterprise.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I agree that we must have private business enterprise. I do not believe that everything should be left to the government. As a matter of fact, one of the great evils in Canada to-day, and for many a day past, has been this spirit of: Oh. let the government do it. We must snap out of that sort of thing. We must get down to encouraging private initiative. That is one of the things that appeals to me under the capitalist system. If you destroy-and now I am looking at my hon. friends to my left- the principle of private initiative in Canada and come to leaning and depending upon paternalism, God help this country.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, one statement just made by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services I cannot agree with. He said that the men of to-day in Nova Scotia are not the equal of their grandfathers. They may not have the experience in shipbuilding, but I believe that if the responsibility is placed upon them, they will prove worthy of their forebears.
It is agreed that the need to-day for ships is greater than in the last war, and the effort being put forth at the present time in building ships in Nova Scotia does not compare with what 'was done there in the last war when there were in that province scores of shipyards building wooden ships. There has been a tremendous development in the use
of diesel engines, so that the wooden ship is to-day far more serviceable than it was in the last war.
Nor is Nova Scotia doing to-day what she did in the last war in building steel ships. A new shipyard was established in Pietou county and several large steel ships were built in the last war. Plates and frames were rolled there to build these ships. During the last war several million dollars were expended in Sydney to roll plates in order that ships might be built in Nova Scotia, but that plate mill is not operating at this time. There is no comparison between the need for ships to-day and in the last war, nor is there any comparison between what has been done to enable Nova Scotia to build ships to-day and what was done in the last war.

My constituency is a
wooden shipbuilding constituency, and I would hate the impression to go out that we have not been building some ships. We have built seine boats and speed boats of various kinds and scows for the government.
I cannot agree with the hon. member for Weyburn when he says: Mobilize those shipbuilders and tell them what to do. If that is the spirit of the west, it is not the spirit of the maritimes. Our shipbuilders do not need to be told what to do.

The difficulty with regard to mine-sweepers has been largely one of finance or occupation on other projects. As I stated in the house the other day, in my constituency or in the constituency adjoining we have an order for two Fairmiles and four mine-sweepers, and we would have undertaken to build more mine-sweepers but for the fact that some of these family shipyards have not the financial resources to go ahead and take a chance on losing from $50,000 to $75,000 or are busy on other work. Their financial build-up is, I think, being remedied. I personally have been working for months trying to get people interested financially and endeavouring to work up enthusiasm, but until sufficient enthusiasm and finances have been developed, we are going to have the situation we have at the present time.
